consensus_summary: The terms chiefly identify the humble, lowly, and dependent faithful—the anawim—who rely on God rather than wealth, status, power, or self-sufficiency and are promised divine deliverance and the kingdom.
book_summary: The terms identify people bowed and empty-handed before God, receptive to the gospel and kingdom because they are not self-sufficient.
consensus_core_identification: Humble and needy people who depend upon God and receive his salvation.
book_core_identification: Humble and empty-handed people who depend upon God and can receive the gospel and kingdom.
boundary_disagreement: No material boundary disagreement. The book emphasizes receptivity and contrasts the group with the rich or self-sufficient, while the consensus more explicitly acknowledges that the language can also denote literal socioeconomic poverty.
material_contradiction: None. The book restates the consensus’s primary spiritual-humility and dependence-on-God identification.
rationale: Both readings center on the same referent: lowly, humble, dependent people who trust God rather than themselves and consequently receive divine favor, the gospel, and the kingdom. The book’s imagery of being “bowed and empty-handed” is a concise formulation of the consensus concept of the anawim. Its contrast with the rich corresponds to the consensus contrast with wealth and self-sufficiency rather than replacing the referent.
strongest_objection: Calling “Rich” the unqualified opposite may imply a sharper exclusion of materially wealthy people and may spiritualize passages about concrete poverty more strongly than the broader consensus permits. However, this does not materially alter the entry’s central identification.
